title: Do You Need a License to Run a Support Group?
summary: Do you need a license to run a support group? No, not for a nonclinical group. Where the line falls, and what you can and cannot call yourself.
body_markdown:
No. You do not need a professional license simply to run a nonclinical support group.


A support group becomes a different kind of service when someone begins assessing, diagnosing, treating, or presenting it as clinical group therapy. That is where the license question actually lives. What also depends on your credentials is what you call yourself, because several professional titles are protected by law.


This page is general information rather than legal advice, and state rules vary. If you are close to one of the lines below, check yours.


## The distinction everything rests on


**MentalHappy hosts expert-led psychoeducational support groups. We do not host group therapy, and nothing on our platform is treatment.**


A support group shares information, builds skills and creates community around a common experience. It is psychoeducational and supplemental. Nobody is assessed, diagnosed or treated, and running one is not a regulated activity.


Group therapy is clinical treatment. It is delivered by a licensed clinician, works from a treatment plan, and has clinical goals. It requires the relevant education, license, supervised training and professional standing.


Almost every question about licensing resolves once you are clear which of those two you are running. Run the first and the licensing question mostly goes away. Drift toward the second and no amount of careful wording protects you.


It helps to think about it from the member's side. Someone joining a support group expects to be among people who understand what they are going through, and to leave with ideas and company. Someone entering treatment expects a professional to assess them and work on their problem. If the people in your room could reasonably believe the second thing is happening, the label on the door will not save you, and they may delay getting care they actually need.


## What you can do without a license


Plenty, and this is the part new leaders underestimate.


- Convene a group around a shared experience and set its purpose
- Facilitate discussion, set ground rules and hold the structure of a session
- Share your own experience, if you have lived the thing the group is about
- Provide information from reputable public sources
- Signpost people to professional help, helplines and community services
- Charge for your time, the structure you provide and the space you create


What makes all of this lawful is not a loophole. It is that none of it is treatment. You are not assessing anyone, you are not forming a clinical judgment about them, and you are not taking responsibility for their care. You are hosting a structured conversation between people with something in common, which is a thing communities have always done.


That last item, charging, surprises people, so it gets its own section below.


## Where the line is


These are the things that turn a support group into something regulated. Avoid them unless you hold the relevant license.


- Diagnosing, or offering an opinion that functions as a diagnosis, including casual versions like “that sounds like depression”
- Delivering a named therapeutic modality as treatment
- Writing anything resembling a treatment plan, or describing members as patients
- Advising someone on medication, including whether to continue or stop
- Presenting the group as a substitute for care someone already has


The common failure is not a dramatic one. It is a leader who knows a lot, wants to help, and gradually starts answering clinical questions because nobody else in the room can. Notice that drift and name it out loud when it happens.


A phrase worth having ready: “I can't advise on that one, and I don't want to guess with something this important, but let's find you someone who can.” It is not a brush-off. Said warmly, in front of the group, it teaches everyone where the edges are, and it models that asking for proper help is normal rather than a failure.


## What to call yourself


Titles carry legal weight. Therapist, psychologist, counselor and social worker are protected in most states: using one without the license behind it is a real offense, not a style issue.


### Titles that describe the role accurately


- Support group facilitator
- Group leader
- Community group organizer
- Peer facilitator, if your standing genuinely comes from lived experience


### Titles to avoid unless licensed


- Therapist, psychotherapist, counselor, psychologist, social worker
- Anything with “clinical” in it
- Trauma specialist, recovery expert, mental health coach: all vague enough to imply clinical standing


Apply the same test to the group's name. “Anxiety Therapy Group” makes a claim. “Anxiety Support Group” does not.


The same goes for how you describe the group in writing. Words like treatment, clinical, therapeutic program, healing protocol and recovery plan all imply something regulated. Support, psychoeducational, facilitated, shared experience and community do not. This matters more than people expect, because your group description is often the only thing a prospective member reads before deciding what they are walking into.


## Can you charge for it?


Yes. You are charging for your time, the structure and the space, not for treatment. Say that plainly in your description so nobody joins expecting clinical care.


Two practical cautions. Do not describe a paid group in terms that imply clinical outcomes. And do not bill insurance for a psychoeducational group; insurance billing is for clinical services, and misbilling is a different and more serious problem than a loose title.


On what to charge, there is no standard rate. It depends on whether an organization is funding the group, whether you are covering your own time, and what the people you want to reach can sustain. Free removes every barrier and tends to produce softer attendance. A small fee usually improves commitment. A high fee changes who can come, which may be a trade you are willing to make or may quietly defeat the point of the group.


If cost is the only thing stopping a group from existing, non-profits, universities, colleges, school administrators and advocacy groups can apply to have a group sponsored so it runs free.


## If you are licensed


Your license does not disappear when you run a support group, and that cuts both ways.


You can run a psychoeducational group, and it is not therapy simply because you hold a license. But your board may still hold you to professional standards in how you conduct it, and the people in the room may assume a clinical relationship exists whether or not you intend one. Say explicitly, at the start, which hat you are wearing.


Keep the boundary clean: a support group member is not your client, and if someone in your group needs treatment, refer them out rather than absorbing them into your practice through the group.


Two other things worth settling before you start. Check whether your professional liability cover extends to non-clinical group facilitation, because many policies are written around one-to-one clinical work and the answer is not always obvious. And if you practice across state lines, remember that the rules following your license may not follow your support group in the same way. That is another question for a lawyer rather than a forum.


## Questions about licensing


### Do I need a license to run a support group?


In most of the United States, no. A support group is psychoeducational, not clinical treatment, and running one is generally not a licensed activity. What does depend on your credentials is what you call the group, what you call yourself, and whether you stay out of diagnosis and treatment. State rules vary, so check yours if you are close to a line.


### Can I charge for a support group if I am not licensed?


Yes. You are charging for your time, the structure and the space, not for treatment. Be clear in your description about what the group is and is not, and do not bill insurance for it. Insurance billing is for clinical services.


### What can I not do without a license?


Diagnose, deliver a therapeutic modality as treatment, write treatment plans, advise on medication, or present the group as a replacement for care. The line is not about how much you know; it is about what the activity legally is.


### Is it different if I have lived experience rather than a qualification?


Lived experience is a legitimate basis for leading a group and it is what many of the best facilitators bring. It does not change the rules above. Share your experience freely; do not convert it into clinical advice for someone else.


### What should I call myself?


Something that describes the role: support group facilitator, group leader, community group organizer. Avoid therapist, counselor, psychologist and social worker unless you hold that license, and avoid vague titles like “mental health coach” that imply clinical standing without claiming it outright.
